title: Antioquia/Choco window meter
description:
A standard electric meter with a second box (metal or plastic), located on one side or above or below it.
The meter is fairly common and very reliable; I've never seen one anywhere other than in these two provinces.

title: Antioquia/North Santander small window meter
description:
A meter with a small window (often with a cover).
In Antioquia, there’s often a second box underneath.
I’ve seen this type of meter once in Santander.

title: Boyaca meter
description:
A meter with two compartments, one of which has a window (rectangular in height).
The second compartment is rarely located on top; very often, there is a small, rounded handle on both compartments.

Note: A meter that could be confused with this one is common in Santander.

title: Santander variant of the Boyaca meter
description:
This meter is therefore very similar to the one from Boyaca; the only difference is in the window, which (to my knowledge) will never be a vertical rectangle but will always be either horizontal or square.
This is a very common and very reliable meter, provided it is clearly distinguishable.

title: Santander rounded window meter
description:
A metal meter with a window that is often oval, sometimes rounded.
The oval window is generally reliable (seen only once in North Santander).

The round window is unreliable; it has already been seen in various places.

title: Cauca/Valle del Cauca meters
description:
A square metal meter; the key feature is the window, which is rectangular with rounded corners and fairly narrow.

The window can sometimes be rectangular and more or less narrow.
A square window is not relevant in this case.

Probably the most common type of meter, but with a fairly wide range. This meter has already been seen in Putumayo. It is also common in Tumaco.

title: Square meter
description:
A square metal counter with a central window.
This type of counter is most commonly found in the Andes, Huila, and Cundinamarca. If the window is very large, it is most likely located in Cundinamarca.

title: Mini door meter
description:
A square metal counter with a window in the upper-left corner and a small door on the right.
This counter was previously seen in Putumayo.

title: Quindio saloon meter
description:
An excellent meter; it has a second gate attached to the right.
The province is small, so it doesn't come up often, but it's very, very strong.
I've never seen it anywhere else.

title: Caqueta small window meter
description:
A square metal meter with a small, off-center window.
A nice meter, not all that common.
I saw one once in Huila.

title: Putumayo meter
description:
A rectangular metal meter with a rounded window.
It is therefore very similar to the one in Santander, but the difference lies in the window, which almost reaches the edges.
Great for the Sibundoy Valley.

title: Tolima jailed meter
description:
A long metal meter with a rectangular window featuring rounded corners.
The meter is very often located behind bars.

title: Cucuta sub-meter
description:
A metal sub-meter found only in the province of Norte de Santander and almost exclusively in Cúcuta.
Quite rare but very useful.

title: Phone booth meter
description:
A metal sub-meter with a grille like this + a door on the left + three slits on the right. The layout must be exactly like this.
It is found mainly in Tolima, Huila, and Cúcuta.

title: Northern jailed sub-meter
description:
Sub-meters like this can be found in the northern part of the country, generally north of Montería.
They are very common and can be very useful in urban areas where navigation isn't straightforward.

title: Cundinamarca H-shaped lamp attach
description: The lamp's mount is shaped like an H at a 90-degree angle. These lamps are fairly common in Colombia; they can be found in the province of Bogotá as well as in Cundinamarca.

title: Antioquia Metal plate
description: Lamps with rectangular bases are very common in Antioquia, and less commonly found in Córdoba or Sucre.

title: Ibague lamp
description:
This streetlight must be excellent, since it’s the only one of its kind in the city of Ibagué, Tolima.
All the streetlights in the city are like this. However, be aware that other red streetlights do exist.

title: Cali lamps
description:
Cali's green streetlights are everywhere in the city.
Be aware that there are many green streetlights in Colombia.

title: Bucaramanga lamps
description:
More green lights—this time from Bucaramanga.
They're different from the ones in Cali; they look newer and often have two LEDs underneath!

title: Barranquilla holey attach
description: If you're in Barranquilla, there's a good chance you'll see these lamps, which are found all over the city and in the surrounding towns.

title: QR code plates
description:
This one is still very well known to everyone since it’s supposed to be in Barranquilla.
But you can find it in quite a few nearby cities; I’ve even seen them in Riohacha and Plato.

title: Caldas barcode
description:
A plate with a barcode always starts with a letter that can help you guess the region (W = West, L = La Dorada, etc.).
Already seen in northern Risaralda.

title: Huila horizontal plate
description:
This is an excellent plate because it’s unique to Huila and very common.
On the left are the old ones (often 3rd generation), which have been replaced by the new ones on the right.
There may be one or two horizontal plates; the format remains the same—a letter followed by numbers. They come in orange, red, and, rarely, gray.

title: Cundinamarca horizontal plate
description:
Probably the best license plate in the country, always in this format: AP + numbers. It’s blue 95% of the time, but it also comes in yellow and is very, very common.

To my knowledge, it doesn’t exist in cities in the northern part of the province.

title: Orange plate
description:
An orange vertical plate with gray numbers.
It’s known to be a Tolima license plate, but I’ve seen quite a few from Valle del Cauca (in a 75/25 ratio).

title: EEBP yellow plate
description: A yellow plate with “E.E.B.P” written on it. It is very, very rare and, to my knowledge, can be found in three cities: La Hormiga, Santa Ana, and Puerto Asis in the province of Putumayo.

title: Blue on orange stickers
description:
Moving on to the stickers: blue lettering on an orange background indicates the provinces of Caldas and Risaralda (in a 70/30 ratio).

These stickers can be found on a very large number of poles; very often, all you’ll see is faded orange paint (images 2 and 3).

title: Orange on yellow stickers
description:
Orange paint on a yellow background indicates the provinces of Risaralda or Chocó.

You’ll often only see the yellow background, so be careful not to confuse it with other pole markings that will follow.

title: Yellow on blue stickers
description: The most common stickers are found in Valle del Cauca, featuring yellow lettering on a blue background. They’re easy to spot and appear on the vast majority of poles.

title: Black on yellow stickers
description: There are several variations, but a yellow background with black lettering on top is typical of Valle del Cauca—and especially its major cities! You see it quite a bit in Cali, Tulua, and Palmira.

title: White on black stickers
description:
We're staying in Valle del Cauca with these white paintings on a black background.
Very common in the city of Cali; I've seen them twice in northern Cauca.

title: Orange painted letters
description:
An orange painting without a background depicts the provinces of Cundinamarca and Bogotá.
Very, very common and rarely seen elsewhere, it is one of the best paintings.

title: Black on orange stickers
description:
Black lettering on an orange background, quite distinct from Caldas's lettering.
As far as I know, this sticker always starts with an M or a B, followed by several digits.

title: Blue on yellow stickers
description:
A blue symbol on a yellow background represents two provinces: Nariño and Cauca.
In Nariño, you’ll find letters and numbers, whereas in Cauca, to my knowledge, you’ll never find any letters.

title: Cursive yellow/green painting
description:
A fairly distinctive hand-painted design, it comes in bright yellow with no background, green with no background, and yellow on a green background.
There are often between 2 and 5 digits. These stickers indicate the northwestern region of Antioquia. The city of Carepa in this area is the only one to feature the green design (image 2).

title: Narino signs
description:
If you see signs that say “ahorre alkosto” or “mora surco” at street corners, you’re in the province of Nariño.

The sign shown in Image 1 is more common than the second one.

title: Meta street signs
description:
While exploring a bit beyond the Andes, I came across these street signs in Meta; as far as I know, they’re unique to this province.

It’s a standard sign with a white arrow, but there’s a street number written above it in white on a green background.

title: Thatched roofs
description: This type of roof is quite common in Colombia; you’ll see it very often in the Northwest, particularly in Córdoba and Sucre.

title: Nairo Quintana graffitos
description:
The first Colombian to win a Grand Tour and a fan favorite, he is adored in his home country, especially in his hometown of Tunja.

A true source of local pride, murals of the cyclist and his iconic Movistar jersey can often be seen in several villages around Tunja.

title: Black car with antenna
description: You're probably familiar with this car with a Gen 3 antenna that can be found in Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil, but keep in mind that if it's black (the car, not the antenna), you're definitely in Colombia

title: Eje Cafetero jeeps
description: Jeeps are ULTRA POPULAR in Colombia’s Coffee Triangle (Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío), and especially in Quindío. If you see one on the road, keep an eye out; if you see two and the scenery matches, it’s totally free. They’re sometimes decked out in a “Pimp My Ride” style, which is an even stronger clue.
